contentBlocks.text: Welcome to Environmental Science & Engineering. This course studies sustainability and ends in a real capstone engineering-design project — both depend on a single foundational skill: systems thinking.

A system is a set of connected parts that interact to produce an outcome, generally described using three elements: inputs (what goes in), outputs (what comes out), and feedback (how outputs affect future inputs). A forest is a real environmental system: inputs include sunlight, water, and nutrients; outputs include oxygen, biomass growth, and water vapor released back into the air. Thinking in systems means looking at these connections and interactions, not just isolated cause-and-effect. Identify the inputs and outputs for a system you're familiar with — it can be environmental (like a garden) or human-made (like a school).

This systems framework — inputs, outputs, feedback — is the lens the rest of this course uses to study environmental sustainability. Tomorrow we'll apply it to a specific, standard sustainability framework.

objectives: Define a system using inputs, outputs, and feedback
Identify the inputs and outputs of a real, familiar system
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Introduce the systems-thinking framework using the forest example.
2. Discuss inputs/outputs/feedback as the three core elements.
3. Have the child identify inputs/outputs for a familiar system of their choice.
4. Complete the worksheet.
5. Preview tomorrow's topic: the three pillars of sustainability.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use a very simple, concrete system (a plant in a pot: water/sunlight in, growth/oxygen out) before asking the child to identify their own
Ready for more: ask them to identify one feedback loop in their chosen system — how an output might affect future inputs
This is the first lesson of the course — a good moment to frame systems thinking as the lens the whole year builds on
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. A system is a set of connected parts that interact, described by inputs, outputs, and feedback. 2. A garden's inputs might include water/sunlight/soil nutrients; outputs might include food, oxygen, and compostable waste.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses the course's 'systems thinking' description, establishing the foundational framework this course's sustainability and engineering-design content build on.
